palette: aubergine velvet against walnut and ivory
topic: putting the furniture you already own into the staged photo
angle: Every other staging post promises the room changes. This one promises the room stays true to the pieces that are not moving, which is the objection that actually stops a seller from trying it.
visualSummary: Deep blue editorial field. Letterspaced FURNITURE REFERENCE eyebrow with the logo lockup at the top, then a two tone headline and a line of setup. Below it two rounded photo cards stacked vertically, each a wide horizontal band holding one sofa at almost the same scale, which is the whole point of the frame. The upper card is a Stagify render of a luxury living room cropped to the seating: a deep aubergine button tufted velvet sofa with two ivory cushions, flanked by walnut side tables and tall brass and glass lamps, two gilt picture frames above, a marble and walnut coffee table with cut glass decanters across the front. The lower card is the owner's own photograph of that same aubergine tufted sofa with two white cushions, shot straight on against white panelled doors with antiqued mirror glass. Small blue pills read STAGED and YOUR SOFA. Aubergine, walnut, ivory and brass against the blue chrome.

copy.headline: Stage it with the sofa you are keeping.
copy.caption:
Your sofa is staying with the house. Most virtual staging replaces it anyway, and the buyer finds that out at the showing.

Upload a photo of the piece instead. Up to five pieces. The room gets built around what is actually there.

The sofa in the lower photo is the sofa in the upper one. Same aubergine velvet, same diamond tufting, same low wraparound arms. The walnut tables, the ivory chairs and the brass are ours. The sofa is not.

That is the difference between a staged photo and a fantasy. Only one of them survives the viewing.

Furniture reference upload is a Stagify+ feature. The free tier stages a real room from seven presets, no card asked for.

images.note: The empty source room the render was staged from. Not shown in the frame: this post's proof is the sofa match, and a third card would have cost the headline its room.

The render cropped to a 1792x680 band around the sofa, which is what the STAGED card carries. editorial-card's cards are wide and shallow and background-size is cover, so the full 3:4 render centred on the gallery wall and put the sofa behind the caption scrim. Cropping to the sofa also matches its scale to the reference card below, which is what makes the two read as one object. Pixels are untouched; see posts/_work/crop-0817.mjs.

params.additionalPrompt: The dark aubergine button-tufted velvet sofa in the reference photograph belongs to the owner and is staying in the house, so place that exact sofa as the main seating and build the rest of the room around it. Keep its colour, its full diamond tufting and its low wraparound arms exactly as shown. Everything else is walnut, ivory and warm brass.

generation.note: Every defect the reviewer named is reference fidelity rather than a rendering artifact, which is the one axis this post cannot be sloppy on, so the render was opened and judged by eye under rule 4 before it was accepted. The first post to use the product's furniture-reference channel: instagram/lib/images/stagify.js stage() and acquire.js acquirePair() gained a furnitureBuffers passthrough to processStaging's fourth argument.

devilsAdvocate.whyThisOne: Every recent post says the room changes. This one says the room stays true to your things, so the direction of the promise is inverted rather than the feature merely swapped. A before and after is consumed whole and stops at a like; this ends on a question the frame deliberately cannot settle, which is whether the tool would really place the viewer's own sofa.
devilsAdvocate.whyItEarnsAClick: The only way to settle the question is to upload. It also removes the objection that stops a seller tapping every other staging advert, that the render is a lie the buyer catches at the showing.
devilsAdvocate.howItDiffers: Four of the last ten posts are seam splits, two are grids, one a comic, one a stacked card, one a type-first stat, one a swipe deck. None makes an object the subject, and none is a two-object editorial pairing. Aubergine against walnut is also the lowest-chroma pairing the grid has carried; the last five all set brand blue against a warm light neutral.
devilsAdvocate.residualRisk: The post is entirely load-bearing on a visual match. If the reference sofa and the rendered sofa do not read as the same object at 400px, the frame becomes two unrelated AI images and the honesty claim inverts, which is worse than a dull post because checkable claims are this brand's whole position.
runnersUp: i13, 'You moved out. The photos noticed.' Killed for repeating legacy-08 from six days earlier on audience, hook archetype, layout family and idea.
i18, 'One sentence changed this room.' Better click mechanic than the other prompt-bar idea, but the proof sits in a text capsule and it reuses the seam shape.
devilsAdvocate.note: Audience was not a choice today. agents and design are both inside their 2-post cooldown, so every candidate on the list targeted homeowners.

review.sofaMatchVerdict: Reads as the same object at 400px with high confidence. Carrying the match: the saturated plum velvet, the tub Chesterfield silhouette whose arms rise to full back height and sweep round unbroken, a single deep tufted seat slab with no loose cushions, all-over diamond tufting on back and arms and seat at once, and two square ivory pillows in matching positions.
nits: Colour temperature. The photographed sofa is a cool aubergine; the rendered one is warmer and redder, lifted by the two table lamps. The reviewer called this the only discrepancy a sceptical viewer notices at feed size, and rated it a bigger threat than anything the product's QA reviewer named.

At 100% the render's tufting is coarser and shallower than the real sofa's and the arms are stiffer, with a polygonal chamfer at the left arm to seat junction. Invisible by 400px. This is what the QA reviewer scored 85 for, three times.
The book spine on the coffee table is illegible AI glyph mush, about 3px tall in the shipped frame.
The fully tufted apron running to the floor, the real sofa's single most identifying feature, is unavailable in both cards: hidden behind the coffee table above, cropped and scrimmed below.
Worst contrast is the W of Walnut where the caption scrim crosses the pale lamp shade, around 3.4:1 by a blurred-band estimate that is inflated by the glyphs themselves. Large bold type, clears AA.
review.designChanges: The STAGED card's band was re-cut from 1792x780 to 1792x680, raising the bottom edge above two pale armchair backs in the render's near foreground that the deeper band sliced at the card's bottom corners, where at 400px they read as grey lumps rather than furniture.
review.colourNotFixed: The reviewer suggested grading one card to close the colour temperature gap. Deliberately not done. The warmth is real lamplight in the render, and this is a post arguing that a staged photo should survive the viewing; retouching two photographs into agreement to make a fidelity claim look better is the exact thing it accuses everyone else of. The gap stays and the caption claims only what the pixels support.
review.samenessVerdict: Not a rerun. It borrows chrome from 08-15 (blue ground, letterspaced eyebrow, pill-labelled card, white CTA pill) and its stacked-pair rhythm from 08-16, but both panels here are photographs rather than colour panels of text, the aubergine appears in no earlier post, and proving one physical object identical across two photographs is new. The warning is cadence: three of the last five now open on a deep blue ground with an eyebrow and a card, so the next post should break to full bleed or the pale wash.
